summary: This program asks for a temperature in Celsius and keeps asking until the reader types a real number inside the physically possible range of -273.15 to 100, then converts that value to Fahrenheit. It combines a loop with two kinds of checking: one for text that is not a number at all, and one for numbers that are out of range.

lines.text: Stating the allowed range in the prompt itself means the reader knows the rule before making a mistake. Using print rather than println leaves the cursor on the same line, so typing happens right after the colon.
This is a try-with-resources statement: the Scanner is created here and Java automatically closes it when the block ends, however it ends.
The capital-D Double is the object version of double, and unlike a plain double it can hold null to mean "no valid value yet." It is declared outside the loop so it survives after the loop finishes.
An intentionally endless loop. The only ways out are the break below, once a good value arrives, so the user gets unlimited retries.
Reads the whole typed line as text and trim removes any stray spaces at the ends, which would otherwise make a perfectly good number fail to parse.
Turns the text into a number. If the text is not a number, this line throws NumberFormatException instead of returning, and control jumps to the catch below.
The range check. The || means "or," so the value is rejected when it is below absolute zero or above the boiling point of water.

lines.code: System.out.print("Out of range. Enter a value between -273.15 and 100: ");
lines.text: A rejection message that repeats the rule, so the user does not have to scroll back to see what was expected.
Skips the rest of the loop body and starts the next round immediately, which is what asks for input again.
Only a number that survived both parsing and the range check gets stored, so celsius can never hold garbage.
Leaves the endless loop now that a valid value is in hand.
Catches the specific failure from parseDouble. Because the catch sits inside the loop, a typo costs one extra prompt rather than crashing the program.
Calls the conversion function with the validated value. Java automatically unwraps the Double object into the plain double the method expects.
Shows both temperatures in one sentence so the result is self-explanatory.
A final safety net for anything unexpected, such as input ending before a valid number is entered. It reports a friendly message instead of dumping a stack trace.
The conversion lives in its own function so the validation loop in main stays focused on collecting input.
The standard formula. Because celsius is a double, the multiplication happens in decimal first, so the 9/5 division does not lose the fraction.
